title: The seven jurists of Medina
hook: scholars of the city who kept the Prophet's practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasan al-Basri, the preacher of Basra who said we are nothing but days. Your line was: watch the heart. What did you catch moving in yours? Day nine hundred nine.

Where do you go to learn how the Prophet prayed, once the people who prayed beside him are gone? Books help. But a book can't show you how a hand is raised, or how long a pause is held. For that, people went to a place. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had lived in Medina, and Medina remembered. The children and grandchildren of his Companions grew up on its streets, in the houses where he had eaten and taught. And in the Umayyad years, while Damascus held the government, Medina held something else. Its scholars became famous as a group, and history calls them the seven jurists of Medina. Today: the city that kept the practice.
screen: `HOW DID HE PRAY?` → `A BOOK CAN'T SHOW A PAUSE.` → `MEDINA REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: These men belonged to the generation Muslims call the Followers, the ones who learned from the Companions. Hear a few of their names, because the names tell the story. Urwa ibn al-Zubayr was a nephew of Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and passed on a great deal of what she taught. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad was a grandson of Abu Bakr and, the reports say, grew up in Aisha's care. Kharija was a son of Zayd ibn Thabit, the Companion who wrote down revelation for the Prophet. And Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, the biographers say, was sought out for his learning on hard questions. Each of them stood one step from the Companions themselves. One wrinkle. The lists agree on most of the names, but differ over the seventh. A famous group, and its membership is still debated. What did they do? They answered questions. How do you divide an inheritance? What does a fair sale look like? When people asked, they answered from what the Companions had said and done, and from what Medina still did. When Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz governed the city, the reports say he called its jurists together and promised to act on nothing without their counsel. A later Medinan scholar, Malik ibn Anas, made this a principle: the practice of the people of Medina. For him, what a whole city had done since the Prophet's day was itself a kind of witness. Medina became the city of the practice.
screen: `THE FOLLOWERS OF THE COMPANIONS.` · `ONE STEP FROM THE COMPANIONS.` · `SIX AGREED, THE SEVENTH DEBATED.` · then, large: `THE PRACTICE OF MEDINA.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one sunnah from Medina. Here's one from Aisha. Asked what the Prophet did at home, she said he served his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. Sit with that for a moment. Breathe in. A man whose words shaped a city helped at home. Breathe out. Bring to mind one small task in your own home that someone else usually does. Hold it in mind, and decide when today you'll do it. If you pray, you can carry that intention into your next prayer. The bell holds the time.
The seven jurists of Medina. Scholars of the Prophet's city, students of his Companions, who answered questions from what Medina remembered and still did. Today's word.
screen: `THE SEVEN JURISTS OF MEDINA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the city of the practice. Today, do the one task at home you chose, the way that report from Aisha describes. Day nine hundred nine.

howItsDone: In the Maliki school of law, the practice of the people of Medina is weighed as evidence alongside the hadith, and students in other schools also learn hadith through chains of teachers that pass through Medina.

original.note: Arabic: the seven jurists, the name later scholars gave Medina's group.

what it means: students of the Companions who answered questions from what the Prophet's city remembered and did.
what a scholar hears: Malik's principle of the practice of the people of Medina, and the honest gap over who the seventh jurist was.
